chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Isma'il ibn Marar from Yunus from Mu'awiya ibn 'Ammar who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'From where does the Mutamatti' (one who performs Hajj al-Tamattu') differ from the Mu'tamir (one who performs Umrah)?' He said: 'Indeed, the Mutamatti' is bound to Hajj, but the Mu'tamir, when he finishes from it, goes wherever he wishes. And al-Husayn ibn Ali (peace be upon him) performed Umrah in Dhi al-Hijjah, then departed on the Day of Tarwiyah to Iraq, while the people were departing to Mina. And there is no harm in performing Umrah in Dhi al-Hijjah for one who does not intend Hajj.'

key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: There is no harm / it is permissible
key_terms.مُرْتَبِطٌ: Bound or tied (referring to remaining in the state of Ihram for Hajj)
key_terms.يَوْمَ ٱلتَّرْوِيَةِ: The Day of Tarwiyah (8th of Dhi al-Hijjah)
key_terms.ٱلْمُتَمَتِّعُ: One who performs Hajj al-Tamattu' (combining Umrah and Hajj with a break)
key_terms.ٱلْمُعْتَمِرُ: One who performs Umrah independently, without combining it with Hajj

ai.seo_question: What is the difference between a Mutamatti' and a Mu'tamir in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* delineates the ritual status of the Mutamatti' versus the Mu'tamir, emphasizing that the former remains bound to Hajj rites while the latter is released upon Umrah completion. It provides a practical precedent via Imam al-Husayn (AS), who performed Umrah in Dhi al-Hijjah and departed for Iraq on the Day of Tawriyah, validating Umrah for those not performing Hajj. This distinction is crucial for understanding the flexibility of pilgrimage rituals in Shia fiqh.
